options.a: ABO antigens on red cells using anti-A and anti-B reagents
options.b: ABO antibodies in plasma using A1 and B reagent red cells
options.c: Rh(D) antigen on red cells using anti-D reagent alone
options.d: Unexpected red cell antibodies using group O screening cells

distractorExplanations.b: That describes reverse (serum) typing, which detects isoagglutinins in plasma, not antigens on the patient's red cells.
distractorExplanations.c: Anti-D detects the D antigen in Rh typing; forward ABO typing uses anti-A and anti-B, not anti-D.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes the antibody screen, which detects non-ABO alloantibodies with O cells, not forward ABO typing.

options.a: Patient plasma + group O screening cells I and II
options.b: Patient serum/plasma + A1 and B reagent cells
options.c: Patient serum + anti-human globulin and check cells
options.d: Patient red cells + anti-A/B

distractorExplanations.a: O screening cells are used in the antibody screen to detect unexpected antibodies, not in reverse ABO typing.
distractorExplanations.c: AHG and check cells belong to the indirect antiglobulin phase; reverse typing is read at immediate spin with A1/B cells.
distractorExplanations.d: Forward typing.

options.a: Negative antibody screen with known history of no transfusion
options.b: ABO forward and reverse results that agree on repeat testing
options.c: Strong 3+ D-positive reaction at immediate spin with a negative control
options.d: Weak D / discrepant D that may require further testing

distractorExplanations.b: Concordant forward and reverse ABO results are the expected finding and raise no D-typing concern.
distractorExplanations.c: A clear-cut D-positive reaction with a valid control is an unambiguous result that needs no further D workup.
distractorExplanations.a: Less urgent than D discrepancy.

ascp-mls-readiness-check-blood-bank-003.explanation: Weak D interpretation affects RhIG and transfusion decisions; follow current AABB/lab policy. Further testing follows laboratory policy.

options.a: Expected ABO isoagglutinins using A1 and B cells
options.b: Unexpected RBC antibodies using screening cells
options.c: IgG or complement already bound to the patient's red cells
options.d: Donor red cell antigens using commercial antisera

distractorExplanations.a: Detecting anti-A and anti-B with A1 and B cells is reverse typing; the screen looks for unexpected non-ABO antibodies.
distractorExplanations.c: Antibody bound in vivo to patient RBCs is detected by the DAT; the screen detects free antibody in plasma by IAT.
distractorExplanations.d: Typing donor cells with antisera is antigen typing; the antibody screen tests patient plasma against reagent O cells.

options.a: It detects IgG antibodies that may not agglutinate in saline
options.b: It detects IgM antibodies that agglutinate best at room temperature
options.c: It enhances agglutination by reducing the zeta potential of red cells
options.d: It confirms ABO grouping when forward and reverse types disagree

distractorExplanations.b: IgM antibodies agglutinate directly at immediate spin or room temperature; AHG is needed to detect IgG coating.
distractorExplanations.c: Reducing zeta potential is the role of enhancement media such as LISS or PEG, not the antiglobulin reagent.
distractorExplanations.d: ABO discrepancies are resolved with repeat testing, A1 lectin and other workups; AHG targets IgG alloantibodies.

options.a: Patient serum/plasma vs donor red cells
options.b: Patient plasma vs reagent O screening cells
options.c: Patient cells vs patient serum only
options.d: Donor serum vs patient cells

distractorExplanations.b: Testing plasma against reagent O cells is the antibody screen; the crossmatch uses the actual donor unit's red cells.
distractorExplanations.c: Autocontrol.
distractorExplanations.d: Minor XM (less used routinely now).

options.a: Leukoreduced and/or CMV-seronegative per policy
options.b: Irradiated to inactivate CMV in donor lymphocytes
options.c: Washed to remove plasma containing CMV antibodies
options.d: Selected from donors with a positive CMV IgG antibody

distractorExplanations.b: Irradiation prevents TA-GVHD by disabling donor lymphocytes; it does not reduce CMV transmission risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Washing removes plasma proteins to prevent allergic reactions; donor CMV antibodies are not the transmission risk.
distractorExplanations.d: CMV-IgG-positive donors carry latent virus in leukocytes; CMV-safe units come from seronegative donors or leukoreduction.

options.a: An acquired B antigen from bacterial deacetylation
options.b: A cold-reactive autoantibody causing extra reactions
options.c: A subgroup of A such as A2 with anti-A1 present
options.d: Hypogammaglobulinemia / weak isoagglutinins

distractorExplanations.a: Acquired B causes an extra forward-type reaction, not weak reverse reactions; it is a red cell antigen problem.
distractorExplanations.b: Cold autoantibodies cause unexpected extra reverse reactions, not weaker-than-expected ones.
distractorExplanations.c: A2 with anti-A1 adds an unexpected reverse reaction with A1 cells; it does not weaken the expected reactions.

options.a: Prevent formation of anti-D after exposure to D-positive RBCs
options.b: Treat already formed high-titer anti-D as the sole therapy
options.c: Prevent ABO hemolytic disease when mother and baby are ABO-incompatible
options.d: Prevent formation of anti-c and anti-K after fetal red cell exposure

distractorExplanations.c: RhIG contains anti-D only; it has no role in preventing ABO hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.
distractorExplanations.d: RhIG targets the D antigen; it does not prevent alloimmunization to other antigens such as c or Kell.
distractorExplanations.b: Does not erase established alloimmunization as sole concept.

options.a: Free antibody in plasma reacting with reagent red cells in vitro
options.b: In vivo coating of RBCs with IgG and/or complement
options.c: A clerical or labeling error until proven otherwise by recollection
options.d: Reduced red cell survival from intrinsic membrane defects such as spherocytosis

distractorExplanations.a: That describes the indirect antiglobulin test; the DAT detects antibody already bound to red cells in vivo.
distractorExplanations.c: A positive DAT usually reflects real in vivo sensitization (HDFN, AIHA, transfusion reaction), not a labeling error.
distractorExplanations.d: Hereditary spherocytosis causes hemolysis with a negative DAT; a positive DAT points to immune-mediated coating.

options.a: Group-specific RBCs based on the patient's prior records
options.b: Group O-positive RBCs preferred for every female patient of childbearing age
options.c: Group AB RBCs, since AB is the universal red cell donor
options.d: Group O RBCs (often O-negative for women of childbearing potential)

distractorExplanations.a: Old records cannot confirm an unknown patient's identity; uncrossmatched RBCs are group O until a current type is done.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the policy; O-negative is preferred for females of childbearing potential to avoid anti-D formation.
distractorExplanations.c: AB is the universal plasma donor group; group O red cells are the universal red cell choice.

ascp-mls-readiness-check-blood-bank-013.explanation: O RBCs are universal donor red cells in emergencies; Rh choice follows policy/risk. Rh selection follows the institution's emergency-release policy.

options.a: Ruling out antibodies using negative reactions and considering phase, dosage, and patient history
options.b: Ruling out antibodies using positive reactions with heterozygous cells, ignoring phase of reactivity
options.c: Matching the reaction pattern to one antigen column and stopping without rule-outs or a rule of three
options.d: Ruling out antibodies on heterozygous cells, then confirming the specificity with a single positive cell

distractorExplanations.b: Rule-outs use non-reacting cells, ideally homozygous ones; reacting heterozygous cells cannot exclude an antibody.
distractorExplanations.c: Skipping rule-outs misses additional antibodies; identification needs exclusion plus the rule of three for probability.
distractorExplanations.d: Heterozygous cells can miss dosage antibodies such as Kidd, and one positive cell does not meet the rule of three.

options.a: Febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reactions and CMV transmission
options.b: Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease and bacterial contamination
options.c: Allergic urticarial reactions and anaphylaxis in IgA-deficient patients
options.d: Transfusion-related acute lung injury and circulatory overload

distractorExplanations.b: TA-GVHD is prevented by irradiation, not leukoreduction, and bacterial contamination is not addressed by WBC removal.
distractorExplanations.c: Allergic and anaphylactic reactions come from plasma proteins; washed or IgA-deficient products address those.
distractorExplanations.d: TRALI is linked to donor antibodies in plasma and TACO to volume; removing leukocytes prevents neither.

ascp-mls-readiness-check-blood-bank-015.explanation: Removing WBCs decreases FNHTR, CMV risk, and alloimmunization risk. It also reduces HLA alloimmunization.

options.a: Increased GFR from hyperfiltration in early diabetes
options.b: Hepatocellular injury with impaired protein synthesis
options.c: Increased tubular reabsorption of creatinine by the kidney
options.d: Reduced glomerular filtration / impaired kidney function

distractorExplanations.a: Hyperfiltration raises GFR, which lowers serum creatinine; an elevated creatinine reflects reduced filtration.
distractorExplanations.b: Liver injury shows in ALT/AST and synthetic markers; creatinine is cleared by the kidney, not the liver.
distractorExplanations.c: Creatinine is filtered and slightly secreted, not reabsorbed; a rising level reflects falling GFR.

options.a: GGT (and ALP)
options.b: CK (and LD)
options.c: ALT (and AST)
options.d: Lipase (and amylase)

distractorExplanations.a: GGT and ALP are cholestatic or biliary markers; ALT and AST are the ones that track hepatocellular injury.
distractorExplanations.b: CK and LD rise with muscle injury and hemolysis; they are not sensitive or specific markers of hepatocyte damage.
distractorExplanations.d: Lipase and amylase mark pancreatic injury, not hepatocellular damage; ALT is the liver-specific enzyme.

options.a: 1–2 days
options.b: 2–3 weeks
options.c: about 6 weeks
options.d: 2–3 months

distractorExplanations.a: A day-to-day window reflects meter or plasma glucose readings; HbA1c integrates glycemia over the red cell lifespan.
distractorExplanations.b: Two to three weeks is the window of fructosamine (glycated albumin), which reflects albumin's shorter half-life.
distractorExplanations.c: Six weeks underestimates the window; HbA1c reflects the roughly 120-day red cell lifespan, about 2–3 months.

options.a: Immediate reporting after checking for hemolysis/sample integrity
options.b: Repeating on a new draw before any notification, even if that takes hours
options.c: Reporting through the LIS only, without a direct call to the caregiver
options.d: Immediate reporting without checking for hemolysis or EDTA contamination

distractorExplanations.b: Waiting hours for a recollection delays a possibly lethal result; criticals are called promptly once integrity is checked.
distractorExplanations.c: Critical values require direct, documented verbal notification with read-back, not passive electronic reporting.
distractorExplanations.d: Hemolysis and K2EDTA carryover falsely raise potassium, so specimen integrity is checked quickly before the call.

ascp-mls-readiness-check-chemistry-005.explanation: Critical values require rapid verification for preanalytics (hemolysis falsely ↑K+) and clinician notification. Clinical correlation follows the critical-value protocol.

options.a: Causing turbidity/volume displacement errors in some methods
options.b: Releasing intracellular potassium from lysed platelets during clotting
options.c: Binding bilirubin and falsely lowering its measured concentration
options.d: Producing pseudohypernatremia on direct ion-selective electrodes

distractorExplanations.b: That describes pseudohyperkalemia from thrombocytosis, not lipemia; lipemia interferes optically and by volume.
distractorExplanations.c: Lipemia interferes through light scatter and volume displacement, not by binding analytes such as bilirubin.
distractorExplanations.d: Lipemia causes pseudohyponatremia on indirect ISE or flame methods; direct ISE is the method that avoids it.

options.a: Physiologic jaundice of the newborn
options.b: Hemolysis with increased bilirubin load
options.c: Gilbert syndrome with reduced UGT1A1 activity
options.d: Hepatic excretion defect / cholestasis

distractorExplanations.a: Physiologic neonatal jaundice is unconjugated; a conjugated rise in a newborn needs a cholestasis workup.
distractorExplanations.b: Hemolysis overloads conjugation and raises unconjugated bilirubin, not the direct fraction.
distractorExplanations.c: Gilbert syndrome lowers conjugating enzyme activity, so the rise is unconjugated, not direct.

ascp-mls-readiness-check-chemistry-009.explanation: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia points to hepatic/cholestatic pathways; hemolysis raises unconjugated. Hepatocellular disease can also cause conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

options.a: Albumin, globulins, and fibrinogen
options.b: Potassium, calcium, and magnesium
options.c: Ethanol, mannitol, and ketones
options.d: Sodium, glucose, and urea (BUN)

distractorExplanations.a: Plasma proteins drive colloid oncotic pressure but add few osmoles because the molecules are large and few in number.
distractorExplanations.b: These cations are present at low concentrations and add little to osmolality compared with sodium.
distractorExplanations.c: These are added osmoles that create an osmolal gap; they are not the normal main contributors to osmolality.

options.a: Falsely increased glucose due to glycolysis
options.b: Falsely decreased glucose due to glycolysis
options.c: Falsely increased glucose from red cell glucose release
options.d: Unchanged glucose if the tube is kept tightly capped

distractorExplanations.c: Red cells consume glucose rather than release it; prolonged cell contact lowers the result by roughly 5–7% per hour.
distractorExplanations.d: Capping prevents evaporation but not glycolysis; prompt separation or a fluoride tube is what preserves glucose.
distractorExplanations.a: Opposite direction.

options.a: Bone source, as in Paget disease or healing fractures
options.b: Placental source during the third trimester of pregnancy
options.c: Hepatic/biliary source of ALP more than bone alone
options.d: Intestinal ALP release after a fatty meal in group O

distractorExplanations.a: Bone ALP rises without GGT; a concurrent GGT increase points to a hepatobiliary source instead.
distractorExplanations.b: Placental ALP rises in late pregnancy with a normal GGT; GGT co-elevation indicates the liver or biliary tree.
distractorExplanations.d: Intestinal ALP can rise after meals in group O or B secretors, but it does not raise GGT.

options.a: Microcytic, normocytic, or macrocytic
options.b: Hypochromic, normochromic, or hyperchromic
options.c: Regenerative or nonregenerative by marrow output
options.d: Anisocytosis grades from 1+ to 4+ on the smear

distractorExplanations.b: Chromia categories come from MCH/MCHC, not MCV; MCV classifies anemias by red cell size.
distractorExplanations.c: Marrow response is judged by the reticulocyte count, not by the mean cell volume.
distractorExplanations.d: Size variation is measured by RDW or smear grading; MCV is the mean cell volume used to classify anemia.

options.a: Microangiopathic hemolytic process
options.b: Hereditary membrane defect such as spherocytosis
options.c: Megaloblastic anemia from B12 deficiency
options.d: Oxidant injury with Heinz body formation

distractorExplanations.b: Spherocytosis produces spherocytes without central pallor; schistocytes are fragments from shear injury.
distractorExplanations.c: B12 deficiency shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils; fragments point to microangiopathy.
distractorExplanations.d: Oxidant injury produces bite and blister cells with Heinz bodies, not the helmet and triangle fragments of MAHA.

options.a: Increased hypersegmented neutrophils in circulation
options.b: Increased immature neutrophils (bands/metas) in circulation
options.c: Increased reactive lymphocytes with abundant cytoplasm
options.d: Toxic granulation and Döhle bodies without immature forms

distractorExplanations.a: Hypersegmentation is a 'right shift' seen in megaloblastic anemia, the opposite of circulating immature forms.
distractorExplanations.c: Reactive lymphocytes suggest viral infection; a left shift refers to immature neutrophil precursors.
distractorExplanations.d: Toxic changes often accompany infection but are not a left shift unless immature neutrophils increase.

options.a: Isolated factor VII deficiency
options.b: Factor VIII/IX deficiency or heparin effect
options.c: Early vitamin K deficiency or warfarin effect
options.d: Factor XIII deficiency or fibrinogen deficiency

distractorExplanations.c: Warfarin and early vitamin K deficiency prolong the PT first because factor VII has the shortest half-life.
distractorExplanations.d: Factor XIII deficiency leaves PT and aPTT normal, and low fibrinogen prolongs both tests rather than aPTT alone.
distractorExplanations.a: VII prolongs PT.

ascp-mls-readiness-check-hematology-006.explanation: Intrinsic pathway defects and unfractionated heparin prolong aPTT more than PT. Other intrinsic pathway problems can produce the same pattern.

options.a: Fibrinogen breakdown by plasmin without clot formation
options.b: A confirmed deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism
options.c: Reduced fibrinolysis from high plasminogen activator inhibitor
options.d: Fibrin formation and fibrinolysis have occurred (nonspecific)

distractorExplanations.a: D-dimer arises from cross-linked fibrin, so a clot must have formed; fibrinogen lysis alone yields other FDPs.
distractorExplanations.b: D-dimer is sensitive but nonspecific; elevation needs imaging to confirm VTE, while a normal level helps exclude it.
distractorExplanations.c: Impaired fibrinolysis would lower D-dimer generation; elevation means plasmin has degraded cross-linked fibrin.

options.a: Iron deficiency anemia by measuring stored iron
options.b: Hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell disease/trait
options.c: Hereditary spherocytosis by red cell membrane analysis
options.d: G6PD deficiency by red cell enzyme activity

distractorExplanations.a: Iron status is assessed with ferritin and iron studies; electrophoresis separates hemoglobin variants.
distractorExplanations.c: Spherocytosis is diagnosed with osmotic fragility or EMA binding, not hemoglobin electrophoresis.
distractorExplanations.d: G6PD deficiency is an enzyme defect detected by enzyme assays; hemoglobin structure itself is normal.

options.a: Bone marrow increases RBC production
options.b: Erythropoietin production falls in renal disease
options.c: Marrow is replaced in aplastic anemia
options.d: Untreated iron deficiency limits hemoglobin synthesis

distractorExplanations.b: Low erythropoietin in kidney disease reduces marrow output, so the reticulocyte count falls.
distractorExplanations.c: Aplastic anemia leaves too few precursors, so reticulocytes are low despite the anemia.
distractorExplanations.d: Untreated iron deficiency gives a low reticulocyte count; it rises after iron is replaced.

ascp-mls-readiness-check-hematology-009.explanation: Reticulocytosis marks marrow response to anemia. Examples include hemolysis or blood loss once iron is available.

options.a: Platelet adhesion/aggregation and vessel wall
options.b: Plasmin-mediated breakdown of the fibrin clot
options.c: Fibrin stabilization by factor XIII cross-linking
options.d: Vitamin K–dependent factor cascade

distractorExplanations.b: Plasmin breakdown of fibrin is fibrinolysis, the final phase after clot formation, not primary hemostasis.
distractorExplanations.c: Factor XIII cross-linking stabilizes fibrin at the end of secondary hemostasis, not the platelet plug phase.
distractorExplanations.d: Secondary hemostasis.

options.a: Possible acute leukemia requiring prompt hematopathology workup
options.b: Leukemoid reaction to infection needing follow-up in a few weeks
options.c: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia needing routine outpatient follow-up
options.d: Iron deficiency with marrow stress needing an iron trial first

distractorExplanations.b: Leukemoid reactions show a left shift with few or no blasts; blasts with cytopenias need urgent workup.
distractorExplanations.c: CLL shows mature small lymphocytes and smudge cells, not blasts; blasts with cytopenias suggest acute leukemia.
distractorExplanations.d: Iron deficiency shows microcytic hypochromic cells, not blasts; delaying workup for an iron trial is unsafe.

options.a: Polycythemia from increased red cell mass
options.b: Inflammation (also anemia, pregnancy, etc.)
options.c: Sickle cells and spherocytes on the smear
options.d: Low fibrinogen and hypogammaglobulinemia

distractorExplanations.a: A high hematocrit slows rouleaux formation and lowers the ESR; anemia, not polycythemia, raises it.
distractorExplanations.c: Abnormally shaped red cells cannot form rouleaux, so they lower the ESR rather than raise it.
distractorExplanations.d: Fibrinogen and immunoglobulins promote rouleaux; low levels lower the ESR rather than raising it.

options.a: Red due to mycolic acid retaining carbolfuchsin after acid-alcohol
options.b: Purple due to lipopolysaccharide binding the iodine mordant
options.c: Purple/blue due to thick peptidoglycan retaining crystal violet
options.d: Pink/red because the alcohol decolorizer removes crystal violet

distractorExplanations.a: That describes acid-fast staining of mycobacteria, not the Gram reaction of Gram-positive organisms.
distractorExplanations.b: LPS is in Gram-negative outer membranes; Gram-positives retain crystal violet in thick peptidoglycan.
distractorExplanations.d: Losing crystal violet and taking up safranin is the Gram-negative result; Gram-positives resist decolorization.

options.a: Staphylococcus aureus (positive) from other staphylococci
options.b: Enterococcus (positive) from Streptococcus (negative)
options.c: Streptococcus (positive) from Staphylococcus (negative)
options.d: Staphylococcus (positive) from Streptococcus (negative)

distractorExplanations.a: That is the coagulase test; all staphylococci are catalase-positive, so catalase cannot separate them.
distractorExplanations.b: Enterococci are catalase-negative like streptococci; they are separated by bile esculin and 6.5% NaCl.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the reactions; staphylococci produce catalase and bubble with peroxide, streptococci do not.

options.a: Enzyme-labeled conjugates producing a measurable color/signal
options.b: Fluorescent-labeled antibodies viewed under a UV microscope
options.c: Visible agglutination of antibody-coated latex particles
options.d: Radioactive isotope-labeled antigens measured by a gamma counter

distractorExplanations.b: That is immunofluorescence (DFA/IFA); ELISA uses an enzyme label with a chromogenic or chemiluminescent substrate.
distractorExplanations.c: Latex agglutination is a direct visible lattice reaction with no enzyme-substrate signal.
distractorExplanations.d: Isotope labels define radioimmunoassay (RIA); ELISA replaced the isotopes with enzyme labels.

options.a: The organism's minimum bactericidal concentration for the drug
options.b: The exact MIC in µg/mL, read directly from the zone diameter
options.c: Antimicrobial activity against the organism under standardized conditions
options.d: That the antibiotic diffused poorly through the Mueller-Hinton agar

distractorExplanations.a: MBC requires subculturing dilution tubes to show killing; disk zones reflect inhibition of growth.
distractorExplanations.b: Zone sizes are interpreted as S/I/R with CLSI breakpoints; an MIC number needs a dilution or gradient method.
distractorExplanations.d: Poor diffusion would shrink the zone; a zone of inhibition reflects the drug inhibiting the organism's growth.

options.a: Long-term immunity after vaccination
options.b: Mucosal immunity in secretions
options.c: Recent/primary immune response (often)
options.d: An allergic type I hypersensitivity

distractorExplanations.a: Durable post-vaccination immunity is reflected by IgG; IgM marks the early primary response.
distractorExplanations.b: Mucosal secretions are dominated by secretory IgA, not IgM, so this describes a different class.
distractorExplanations.d: Type I hypersensitivity is mediated by IgE bound to mast cells, not by IgM.

options.a: Multiple sets growing the same Gram-negative rod in a septic patient
options.b: S. aureus in a single bottle from a patient with a central line
options.c: CoNS in two sets drawn from separate sites in a patient with a prosthetic valve
options.d: Single bottle growth of skin flora (e.g., CoNS) with mismatched clinical picture

distractorExplanations.b: S. aureus is rarely a contaminant; even one positive bottle is treated as true bacteremia and worked up.
distractorExplanations.c: CoNS in multiple separately drawn sets with a prosthetic device suggests true infection, not contamination.
distractorExplanations.a: Likely true bacteremia.

options.a: Inhibit Gram-negatives and differentiate mannitol fermentation among staphylococci
options.b: Inhibit Gram-positives and differentiate H2S production among Gram-negatives
options.c: Inhibit Gram-positives and differentiate lactose fermentation among Gram-negatives
options.d: Support all bacteria and differentiate hemolysis patterns on sheep blood

distractorExplanations.a: That describes mannitol salt agar, which selects for staphylococci with high salt, not MacConkey.
distractorExplanations.b: H2S differentiation is a feature of HE or XLD agar; MacConkey differentiates by lactose fermentation.
distractorExplanations.d: Blood agar is an enriched nonselective medium for hemolysis; MacConkey is selective for Gram-negatives.

options.a: Specific antibodies to separated protein antigens
options.b: Specific DNA sequences transferred to a membrane
options.c: Specific RNA transcripts separated by gel electrophoresis
options.d: Viral RNA load by amplification and real-time detection

distractorExplanations.b: DNA transferred to a membrane and probed is a Southern blot; the Western blot detects protein-antibody binding.
distractorExplanations.c: RNA detection on a membrane is the Northern blot; immunoblots probe separated proteins with patient antibody.
distractorExplanations.d: Quantitative viral load uses NAAT such as RT-PCR, not antibody reactivity to separated proteins.

ascp-mls-readiness-check-micro-immuno-01.explanation: Immunoblots detect Ab reactivity to specific proteins after separation. Older HIV testing algorithms used it as the confirmatory step.

options.a: Anaerobic stool culture alone, without any toxin confirmation step
options.b: Testing of formed stool to screen for colonization
options.c: Stool ova and parasite exam with modified acid-fast stain
options.d: Stool testing for toxins and/or toxin gene NAAT per algorithm

distractorExplanations.a: Culture also grows nontoxigenic strains and is slow; diagnosis requires toxin or toxin-gene detection.
distractorExplanations.b: Formed stool is rejected; testing is limited to unformed stool to avoid detecting mere colonization.
distractorExplanations.c: O&P and acid-fast stains target parasites such as Cryptosporidium, not toxigenic C. difficile.

options.a: Testing patient isolates in duplicate on the same day
options.b: Testing ATCC strains once at installation of a new disk lot
options.c: Testing appropriate ATCC control strains with acceptable ranges
options.d: Testing ATCC control strains and reading zones against patient breakpoints

distractorExplanations.a: Duplicate patient testing checks reproducibility but cannot verify accuracy; QC uses reference strains with known ranges.
distractorExplanations.b: QC is run at a defined frequency (daily, or weekly under a validated plan), not just when a new lot is installed.
distractorExplanations.d: QC zones are compared with the CLSI QC range for the reference strain, not with clinical S/I/R breakpoints.

options.a: Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii in CSF/serum contexts
options.b: Histoplasma capsulatum in bone marrow or urine
options.c: Candida albicans in CSF with germ tube testing
options.d: Pneumocystis jirovecii in bronchoalveolar lavage

distractorExplanations.b: Histoplasma is detected by urine antigen and culture; India ink highlights the cryptococcal capsule.
distractorExplanations.c: Germ tube testing identifies Candida albicans; India ink and CrAg target encapsulated Cryptococcus.
distractorExplanations.d: Pneumocystis is shown with GMS, calcofluor, or DFA staining, not India ink or cryptococcal antigen.
